analysis.investment_thesis: Kirloskar Pneumatic is a genuinely sound industrial business with a 15+ year earnings record and near-zero debt — exactly the type of enterprise I admire. However, at P/E 42x and P/B 7.15x, the price is nearly three times my Graham Number of ~INR 358, leaving no margin of safety whatsoever.
key_strengths: Virtually debt-free (D/E 0.01) with consistent earnings through multiple cycles, including the 2015 industrial downturn
15+ years of unbroken profitability; net profit compounded from INR 18 Cr (2015) to INR 211 Cr (2025)
Strong free cash flow generation — INR 137 Cr in FY2025 with OCF positive all 5 years
key_risks: P/E of 42x is nearly 3x my upper threshold of 15x — any earnings disappointment could cause severe price compression
P/B of 7.15x means paying INR 7 for every INR 1 of net assets; book value provides zero cushion to the buyer
Revenue dipped 34% from INR 666 Cr (2012) to INR 441 Cr (2015), revealing cyclical industrial demand exposure
red_flags: Graham Number ≈ INR 358 (sqrt(22.5 × EPS ~32.5 × BVPS ~175)); current price of INR 1,263 is 3.5x the Graham Number — no margin of safety
EV/EBITDA of 29x embeds aggressive growth assumptions that the market, not the buyer, will capture
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I find the underlying business commendable by my standards. Kirloskar Pneumatic has earned money consistently for over fifteen years, carried virtually no debt (borrowings INR 9 Cr against equity of INR 1,139 Cr), and converted earnings into cash reliably — operating cash flow of INR 215 Cr in FY2025 against net profit of INR 211 Cr is precisely the honest earnings quality I seek. ROCE of 24.49% and an operating margin of 17.52% suggest a business with some competitive advantage in its niche. This is the kind of enterprise I might place in my "approved" list for consideration.

The difficulty is entirely one of price. At INR 1,263, the market is asking me to pay 42 times earnings and 7.15 times book value. My Graham Number works out to roughly INR 358 — the current price is 253% above that level. Mr. Market, in his present enthusiasm for Indian industrials and the capex cycle narrative, has priced this stock for near-perfection. I am not in the business of paying for perfection; I am in the business of buying sound businesses at prices that protect me if I am wrong. Here, there is no such protection. Should earnings stall — as they did sharply in 2015 — or should interest rates rise, this multiple would compress violently. I require a price closer to INR 400–500 before I would consider this investment worthy of the disciplined investor's capital.
